interest:
I study JWST observations of high-redshift galaxies and AGN, especially
little red dots (LRDs), compact red sources, dust-reddened or broad-line AGN,
early black-hole growth, and galaxy/AGN co-evolution at cosmic dawn.

Prioritize papers about:
1. JWST/NIRCam/NIRSpec/MIRI observations of high-redshift galaxies and AGN
2. little red dots, compact red galaxies, obscured AGN, broad-line AGN, and
   high-redshift black hole candidates
3. SED fitting, spectroscopy, emission lines, photometric redshifts, stellar
   masses, dust attenuation, AGN contamination, and source classification
4. high-redshift galaxy formation, reionization-era galaxies, early SMBH
   growth, and galaxy/AGN co-evolution
5. survey papers from CEERS, JADES, UNCOVER, COSMOS-Web, PRIMER, GLASS,
   RUBIES, and similar JWST deep fields

Also keep papers about AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs),
large multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, anomaly detection,
automated classification, spectral/photometric inference, or research agents
when they are applied to astronomy, astrophysics, JWST data, galaxy surveys,
AGN selection, or literature/data analysis.

Deprioritize unrelated stellar, solar-system, local-universe, gravitational
wave, or purely theoretical papers unless they directly inform high-redshift
galaxies, AGN, JWST analysis, or AI-for-astronomy workflows.

papers.title: Supermassive Black Hole Assembly from Heavy Seeds with Dynamical Friction in the BRAHMA Simulations: Implications for JWST, LISA, and the Local Universe
papers.authors: Aklant K. Bhowmick , Laura Blecha , Paul Torrey , Luke Zoltan Kelley , Rachel S. Somerville , Rainer Weinberger , Priyamvada Natarajan , Tiziana Di Matteo , Lars Hernquist , Mark Vogelsberger , Alex M. Garcia
papers.abstract: The JWST discoveries of supermassive black holes (BHs) at $z \gtrsim 5$ may provide key insights into their seeding origins. Using new $[18{-}72~\rm Mpc]^3$ BRAHMA cosmological simulations, we investigate how variations in heavy-seed prescriptions, coupled with a subgrid dynamical friction model, shape BH populations at $z \sim 5$ and $z \sim 0$. We consider two "lenient'' seed models, in which all halos containing sufficient dense & metal-poor gas form $\sim10^4$ and $\sim10^5~M_{\odot}$ seeds, and a "strict'' seed model, in which $\sim10^5 M_{\odot}$ seeds form only under additional constraints motivated by direct collapse black hole formation. By $z \sim 5$, all models produce $M_*-M_{\rm BH}$ relations broadly consistent with the observed local Universe for $M_*\gtrsim10^9~M_{\odot}$ galaxies, but only the lenient scenarios generate systems near the upper envelope of the observed local scatter. In galaxies hosting $M_{\rm BH} \sim 10^8$-$10^9~M_{\odot}$ BHs, lenient production of $\sim10^5~M_{\odot}$ seeds also produces multiple overmassive systems with $M_{\rm BH}/M_* \gtrsim 0.01$. Although their growth is dominated by seeding and mergers, these systems reach luminosities of $\sim10^{43}$-$10^{45}\mathrm{erg s^{-1}}$, comparable to those inferred for JWST-detected BHs. As a key observational signature, the lenient seed models yield merger rates of $\gtrsim100\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ and near-unity local BH occupation fractions even in galaxies with $M_* \lesssim 10^7~M_{\odot}$. In contrast, the strict seed model produces merger rates of only $\sim1\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ and local occupation fractions of $\lesssim10\%$ for galaxies with $M_* \lesssim 10^8~M_{\odot}$. Future gravitational-wave event rates and measurements of local BH occupation fractions will therefore provide strong constraints on the dominant pathways responsible for high-redshift BH assembly.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses supermassive black hole assembly from heavy seeds at high redshift, comparing to JWST detections and predicting LISA merger rates, perfectly aligned with all research interests.
papers.Short digest: How do heavy-seed prescriptions shape BH populations at z~5 and z~0 in cosmological simulations? Lenient seed models produce overmassive BHs with luminosities comparable to JWST-detected sources and high merger rates, while strict models yield low occupation fractions. This matters because it provides testable predictions for JWST, LISA, and local BH demographics that can distinguish seeding pathways.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the M_*-M_BH relations at z~5 and compare to JWST constraints
Look for the predicted BH merger rates and occupation fractions for low-mass galaxies
Examine the luminosities and Eddington ratios of simulated BHs compared to observed JWST AGN

papers.title: Unprecedented Constraints on Gas Flows at High Redshift Using Deep JWST/NIRSpec Observations from the LyC22, EXCELS, and AURORA Surveys
papers.authors: Emily Kehoe , Alice E. Shapley , Adam C. Carnall , Fergus Cullen , Thomas M. Stanton , Daniel Schaerer , Rui Marques-Chaves , Charles C. Steidel , Ryan L. Sanders , Natalie Lam , Karla Z. Arellano-Cordova , Ryan Begley , Sophia R. Flury , Natalia G. Guseva , Timothy Heckman , Alaina Henry , Akio K. Inoue , Yuri I. Izotov , Ho-Hin Leung , Derek J. McLeod , Kate Rowlands , Alberto Saldana-Lopez , Dirk Scholte , Maya Skarbinski , Struan D. Stevenson , Elizabeth Taylor , Bingjie Wang , Naveen A. Reddy
papers.abstract: We investigate how low-ionization gas flows in typical star-forming galaxies at $z\sim3$ depend on galaxy intrinsic properties and viewing angle. For this analysis we use JWST/NIRSpec observations of rest-frame near-UV Fe II and Mg II absorption, and rest-frame optical Na D absorption. This study combines galaxies from the LyC22, EXCELS, and AURORA surveys and contains 176, 197, and 315 galaxies, respectively, with Fe II, Mg II, and Na D coverage. Based on both individual and composite spectra, we find no statistically significant correlations between outflow velocity and galaxy properties. However, galaxies with detected outflows tend towards higher stellar masses, SFR, and $\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$ than those without outflows, suggesting that the two samples are not drawn from the same parent population. Finally, we additionally find that Mg II emission is preferentially detected in galaxies with lower stellar mass and $A_V$, and higher sSFR, consistent with conditions that favor the escape of resonantly scattered line and ionizing continuum radiation. We present the first evidence in $z\sim3$ star-forming galaxies that properties of the absorption lines depend on galaxy inclination, with more face-on systems showing stronger absorption and higher outflow velocities, while inflowing gas is more frequently detected in more highly inclined galaxies. These trends are consistent with observations at $z\lesssim1$ and predictions from cosmological simulations in which galactic winds are launched perpendicular to the galactic disks, while accretion occurs primarily along the disk plane.
papers.Reasons for match: Uses deep JWST/NIRSpec observations to study gas flows in z~3 star-forming galaxies, directly relevant to high-redshift galaxy outflows and accretion.
papers.Short digest: How do low-ionization gas flows in z~3 star-forming galaxies depend on galaxy properties and viewing angle? No strong correlations with outflow velocity are found, but Mg II emission is preferentially detected in lower-mass, lower-A_V galaxies, and absorption-line properties depend on inclination. This matters because it provides the first evidence at z~3 that galactic winds are launched perpendicular to disks, informing models of galaxy evolution and gas escape at high redshift.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the composite spectra for Fe II, Mg II, and Na D absorption profiles
Look for the inclination-dependent trends in absorption strength and outflow velocity
Examine the Mg II emission detection fraction as a function of stellar mass and sSFR

papers.title: Direct detection of cool molecular gas in a star-forming galaxy at $z=7.31$
papers.authors: Karin Cescon , Jacqueline A. Hodge , Leindert A. Boogaard , Hiddo S. B. Algera , Lucie E. Rowland , Dominik A. Riechers , Renske Smit , Ilse De Looze , Rychard Bouwens , Paul van der Werf , Manuel Aravena , Elisabete da Cunha , Pratika Dayal , Andrea Ferrara , Rebecca Fisher , Hanae Inami , Pavel E. Mancera Piña , Pascal A. Oesch , Andrea Pallottini , Matus Rybak , Sander Schouws , Laura Sommovigo , Mauro Stefanon , Livia Vallini
papers.subjects: Astrophysics of Galaxies (astro-ph.GA) ; Cosmology and Nongalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)
papers.abstract: We investigate the molecular gas content and interstellar medium (ISM) conditions of REBELS-25, a massive, star-forming galaxy at $z=7.31$. Deep VLA Q-band and ALMA Band 3 observations reveal CO(3-2) and CO(7-6) emission (both at $\sim3.5\sigma$), and provide an upper limit on [C I](2-1). From the CMB-corrected CO(3-2) flux-representing the highest-redshift detection of a low-$J$ CO transition to date-we derive a molecular gas mass of $M_{\rm mol}=(1.0\pm0.4)\times10^{11}\,(\alpha_{\rm CO}/(3\,$M$_{\odot}$(K$\,$\kms$\,$pc$^2)^{-1}))\,$M$_{\odot}$, directly confirming the presence of a very massive gas reservoir only $\simeq700\,$Myr after the Big Bang. This implies an extreme gas fraction of $f_{\rm gas}\simeq0.95$, a gas-to-dust ratio of $\delta_{\rm GDR}\simeq6\times10^2$, and a depletion timescale of $\tau_{\rm dep}\simeq1.2\,$Gyr, broadly consistent with extrapolated scaling relations for main-sequence galaxies at lower redshift. Using the radiative transfer code TUNER, we self-consistently model CO and dust continuum emission in the context of the significant CMB background, constraining ISM properties and recovering $M_{\rm mol}= (1.8^{+1.0}_{-0.9})\times10^{11}\,$M$_{\odot}$, independent of assumptions about $r_{31}$ and $\alpha_{\rm CO}$. We further discuss the use of alternative molecular gas tracers at early epochs. Combining CO and [C II] measurements, we infer an empirical [C II]-to-H$_2$ conversion factor of $\alpha_{\rm [C II]}=(60\pm25)\,$M$_{\odot}$/L$_{\odot}$, suggesting [C II] remains a viable molecular gas tracer in the Epoch of Reionization. These results demonstrate the detectability of low-$J$ CO emission even at $z>7$, paving the way for next-generation facilities, and provide critical insights into the rapid mass assembly of galaxies during the first billion years of cosmic history.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly detects molecular gas (CO) in a massive star-forming galaxy at z=7.31 using ALMA and VLA, highly relevant to early galaxy formation, gas reservoirs, and ISM conditions at cosmic dawn.
papers.Short digest: This paper asks whether massive gas reservoirs exist in galaxies only 700 Myr after the Big Bang. It reports the highest-redshift detection of low-J CO emission, finding a molecular gas mass of ~10^11 Msun and an extreme gas fraction of ~0.95. This matters because it directly confirms rapid mass assembly in early galaxies and provides constraints on gas-to-dust ratios and depletion timescales.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check CO(3-2) and CO(7-6) spectra and significance levels
Look for CMB correction methodology and radiative transfer modeling with TUNER
Examine derived gas fraction, depletion timescale, and [C II]-to-H2 conversion factor

papers.title: Feedback-Free Star Formation in Clusters within a Galaxy Simulated at High Resolution in Cosmic Dawn
papers.authors: Hou-Zun Chen , Zhaozhou Li , Avishai Dekel , Zhiyuan Yao , Nir Mandelker , Xi Kang
papers.abstract: We perform a cosmological zoom-in simulation of a massive galaxy ($M_s\sim10^{10}\rm M_\odot$ at $z\sim10$) using the GIZMO code. By employing $\leq 3\rm pc$ resolution and a $3.4\rm Myr$ supernova feedback delay, we capture the feedback-free starbursts (FFB) in clusters. The simulation reproduces FFB model predictions and super-bright galaxies observed by JWST. At $z\sim10$, cold streams feed a compact galaxy ($R_{\rm e}\sim1\rm kpc$), with stellar and surface densities ($>10^5\rm cm^{-3}$, $>10^5\rm M_\odot pc^{-2}$) exceeding FFB thresholds. The global star-formation efficiency (SFE) is $\varepsilon_s\sim0.2\text{--}0.3$, associated with a fluctuating star-formation history. We identified over $10^5$ star clusters ($M_{\star}>10^{4.5}\rm M_\odot$) with a nearly scale-free mass distribution (${\rm d}N/{{\rm d}\log M}\propto M^{-1.06}$). Approximately 90\% of star formation occurs in clusters, which at a given time constitute $30\text{--}40\%$ of the total stellar mass. The star formation in most of the clusters of masses $<10^7\rm M_\odot$, occurs in bursts of $<3\rm Myr$ and a local SFE $\sim0.5\pm 0.2$. Cluster metallicities ($-2.01<\log (Z/Z_\odot)<-0.45$) indicate rapid baryon recycling. Feedback-driven outflows exhibit typical temperature of $10^7\rm K$ and typical velocities of $\sim 2000\rm km\ s^{-1}$. In the highly dynamic central $1\rm kpc$, clusters undergo rapid orbital decay and merge to assemble the oblate nuclear stellar cluster. Cluster shapes range from oblate to prolate, with a triaxial median. These clusters are consistent with JWST observations, and a fraction of them may survive to yield the globular clusters (GCs) at low redshifts.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly simulates feedback-free starbursts in a massive galaxy at z~10, reproducing JWST-observed super-bright galaxies and star cluster properties relevant to high-redshift galaxy formation.
papers.Short digest: How do feedback-free starbursts (FFB) shape galaxy formation at cosmic dawn? A cosmological zoom-in simulation with 3 pc resolution reproduces FFB model predictions and JWST-observed super-bright galaxies, showing 90% of star formation occurs in clusters with high local SFE. This matters because it provides a physical model for the compact, dense star-forming systems seen in JWST high-redshift observations.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the simulated stellar mass and surface density distributions against FFB thresholds
Look for comparisons of simulated cluster properties (mass function, metallicities) with JWST observations
Examine the merger timescales and orbital decay of clusters in the central 1 kpc

papers.title: Chemical signatures from the first stars embedded in metal-poor gas in galaxies at cosmic dawn
papers.authors: Clara L. Pollock , Kasper E. Heintz , Elka Rusta , Darach Watson , Stefania Salvadori , Callum Witten , Joris Witstok , Ioanna Koutsouridou , Viola Gelli , Pascal A. Oesch , Gabriel B. Brammer , Andrea Saccardi , Kei Ito , Rashmi Gottumukkala , Dagmar Bergholt , Kasper R. Brooksby , Chamilla Terp , Francesco Valentino
papers.abstract: The first generation of stars formed from pristine, neutral hydrogen gas. The most massive of these exploded as supernovae within a few million years of their birth, producing the first heavier elements and leaving distinct chemical signatures of their origin in the surrounding medium. However, chemical abundance studies have so far mainly relied on emission-line measurements, which are luminosity weighted and hence biased towards the most recently formed stars. Here we analyse near-infrared, medium-resolution spectroscopy from the JWST-SPURS program of three UV-bright galaxies at redshifts 7.8, 8.6, and 9.3, within the first 650 to 520 million years after the Big Bang. The chemical abundance patterns of the metal lines detected in absorption hint at extremely metal-poor gas, substantially lower than inferred from the emission lines tracing the central, star-forming regions. Further, they all exhibit super-solar [C/O] abundances, which is also imprinted in the averaged spectrum of a larger set of galaxies at similar redshifts. These results reveal the distinct chemical signatures of the first Population III supernovae explosions.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly studies high-redshift galaxies (z=7.8-9.3) with JWST/NIRSpec, focusing on chemical signatures of first stars and metal-poor gas, which is relevant to early galaxy formation and ISM conditions at cosmic dawn.
papers.Short digest: This paper asks whether chemical abundance patterns in UV-bright galaxies at z>7.5 retain signatures of the first Population III stars. Using JWST-SPURS medium-resolution spectroscopy, they find extremely metal-poor gas in absorption and super-solar [C/O] abundances, distinct from emission-line measurements. This matters because it provides direct evidence for primordial stellar nucleosynthesis in the reionization era, informing models of early enrichment and galaxy assembly.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check absorption-line measurements and derived abundances for each galaxy
Look for comparison between absorption and emission-line metallicities
Examine the stacked spectrum of the larger galaxy sample for [C/O] trends

papers.title: The X-ray photon index Eddington ratio relation in radio-quiet quasars from XMM-Newton and SDSS
papers.authors: SH. M. Shehata , Baraa Hany , Reham Mostafa
papers.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive X-ray spectroscopic analysis of 642 quasars, obtained by cross-matching the XMM-Newton Serendipitous Source Catalog (DR11) with the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (DR16) quasar catalog. After stringent quality filtering and automated spectral reduction, we derived reliable photon indices ($\Gamma$) and intrinsic 2--10 keV X-ray luminosities. Using multiwavelength data, sources were classified into 561 radio-quiet (RQ) and 81 radio-loud (RL) quasars. We estimate the bolometric luminosity and Eddington ratio ($\lambda_{\mathrm{Edd}}$) from absorption-corrected X-ray measurements and virial black hole masses. Our primary objective is to establish and characterize the fundamental relationship between the photon index and Eddington ratio for RQ population. We find that RQ quasars exhibit systematically higher Eddington ratios, peaking at $\log \lambda_{\mathrm{Edd}} \approx -1.2$, and softer spectra with $\Gamma \approx 2.0$. A statistically significant positive correlation between $\Gamma$ and $\lambda_{\mathrm{Edd}}$ is detected in RQ quasars, supporting disk--corona coupling models. To validate our results within the broader context of AGN evolution, we further examine the dependence of $\lambda_{\mathrm{Edd}}$ on redshift ($z$) and black hole mass ($M_{\mathrm{BH}}$). For RQ quasars, $\lambda_{\mathrm{Edd}}$ increases with redshift and decreases with $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$, in strong agreement with recent results \cite{aggarwal2024evidence}, highlighting the universal nature of these accretion trends. By correlating spectral slope with accretion rate, this work provides new insights into the interplay between accretion physics, jet activity, and the cosmic evolution of quasars.
papers.Reasons for match: Studies the X-ray photon index-Eddington ratio relation in radio-quiet quasars, relevant to AGN accretion physics but at lower redshifts (SDSS) and not JWST-specific.
papers.Short digest: What is the relationship between X-ray photon index and Eddington ratio in radio-quiet quasars? A significant positive correlation is found, supporting disk-corona coupling models. This matters for understanding AGN accretion physics that may apply to high-redshift AGN, but the sample is not high-z.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the redshift distribution of the quasar sample to see if any high-z sources are included
Look for the methodology of Eddington ratio estimation from X-ray and virial masses
Examine whether the Γ-λ_Edd relation is tested at the highest redshifts in the sample

papers.title: Galaxy clusters in the VIDEO fields: detection and characterisation in the context of MOONRISE
papers.authors: Pierre Galois , Christophe Benoist , Gianluca Castignani , Matteo Maturi , Sophie Maurogordato , Pascale Jablonka , Yannick Bahé , Derek McLeod , Rebecca Bowler , Olga Cucciati , Lauro Moscardini , Manuela Magliocchetti , Mario Radovich , Michele Cirasuolo , Giovani Covone , Fergus Cullen , Callum Donnan , Hector Flores , William Hartley , Roberto Maiolino , Ross McLure , Nicolarosario Napolitano , Maurizio Paolillo , Mattia Vaccari
papers.abstract: We analyse the cluster content of the $\sim 4.5 \text{ deg}^{2}$ XMM-LSS and CDFS VIDEO fields which are expected to be partially covered by the upcoming MOONRISE survey. Using AMICO and WaZP photometric redshift-based cluster finders, we construct a sample of $519$ cluster candidates detected by both finders in the redshift range $z = 0.1-3$, including $74$ detections at $z > 1.5$. For all detections, we identify the Brightest Central Galaxy (BCG) and compute a list of probabilistic cluster memberships. Our photometric redshift measurements of the clusters agree well with spectroscopic redshifts from the literature, when available. From ancillary spectroscopic data, we assign $z_\text{spec}$ measurements to $116$ cluster candidates based on their spectroscopic members and to $204$ based on their likely BCGs. We also show that candidates containing Radio-Loud members are efficiently recovered using the prior-based cluster finder PPM. We perform a preliminary analysis of the galaxy content of these candidates, focusing on the Red-Sequence components of their apparent Colour-Magnitude Diagram. By comparing with models of galaxy evolution, we show that this population is consistent with a model of passive evolution with a formation at high redshift, and is already in place at $z = 1.5-2.0$. Finally, our cluster sample is used to evaluate how these clusters would be detected and characterised, according to various MOONRISE strategies. We show that cluster spectroscopic confirmation and characterisation could be efficiently achieved up to $z\sim1.7$ even with the shallowest survey strategy. This open unprecedented insight into the physical properties of high-redshift galaxy clusters and into galaxy formation in dense environments.
papers.Reasons for match: Discusses high-redshift galaxy clusters (z up to 3) using VIDEO fields and MOONRISE survey, relevant to galaxy evolution in dense environments, but not specifically focused on JWST or AGN.
papers.Short digest: This paper constructs a sample of 519 galaxy cluster candidates at z=0.1-3 from VIDEO fields, with 74 at z>1.5. It finds that cluster red sequences are consistent with passive evolution from high redshift. This is moderately relevant as it probes high-redshift galaxy clusters, but lacks JWST data or AGN focus.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check cluster detection methods (AMICO, WaZP) and redshift accuracy
Look for spectroscopic confirmation of high-redshift clusters
Examine red-sequence analysis and comparison with passive evolution models
